newsitem.title: NORWAY: FEATURE - Norway billionaire eats humble pie.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Norway billionaire eats humble pie.

text.p: Billionaire Kjell Inge Roekke dropped plans to build a luxurious holiday house on an island near Oslo after angering his fellow Norwegians who felt he was flaunting his wealth.
"I don't want to mess with the soul of the Norwegian people," said Roekke, an entrepreneur whose rags-to-riches career has been frontpage news for the past year.

"The house...would have been useful and great fun for myself, my family and my friends. But my purchase (of the island) has obviously been a pest and a plague to many," Roekke told the financial daily Dagens Naeringsliv. "Enough is enough."
Roekke has fallen foul of "Jantelaw", an expression coined by the late Norwegian author Aksel Sandemose to describe the petty social control in a small town.
"You must not believe you are someone," reads the first of 10 "commandments" in Sandemose's book, published in 1933.
"You must not believe you are better than us," another says.

The "Jantelaw" mentality is believed to have its roots in Protestant puritanism, the historical absence of an aristocracy in Norway and the egalitarian values of the Social Democrats who for decades have dominated political life in Scandinavia.
Roekke, 38, began his career as a penniless 17-year-old on a fish factory trawler in the Arctic. Today his seafood business is the world's largest white-fish fishing and processing operation.
His investment group RGI, one of Norway's youngest firms, last year merged with the industrial group Aker, one of Norway's oldest companies, to form a big player on the corporate scene.
DISAPPROVAL OF EXTRAVAGANT LIFESTYLE
Many Norwegians disapprove of the lifestyle of people like Roekke -- whose hobbies include speedboat racing and travelling in his private jet -- whom they regard as upstarts.

"We need laws that come into effect when some individuals lose contact with Earth and take to the skies," Yngve Haagensen, leader of the powerful Confederation of Trade Unions (LO), said in a Labour Day speech. "Ordinary people don't understand the point of having luxury-class cabins, houses, boats and cars."

The German essayist Hans Magnus Enzensberger in 1984 summed up Norwegian attitudes on private consumption in "Norwegian Anachronisms", a book which has become a classic for observers of Norway, a country of 4.3 million tucked away in the northern backwaters of Europe.

"The clocks have always ticked differently in Norway," he wrote. "Private consumption in Norway is rather seen as a necessary evil, and there is just a hairline border separating it from sinful excesses. Where the permitted ends and the sinful begins is a question it takes considerable moral sensitivity to answer.
"A wealthy citizen would rather anchor his yacht in a remote corner of the bay than face the risk of annoying his neighbour with the provocative pop of a champagne cork," Enzensberger wrote.

While Roekke now plans to sell his 10-million-crown ($1.4 million) island, he said he would not stop the construction of a big yacht for himself, adding: "This boat is not being built in Norway and it will probably be sailed in foreign waters".
"I realise that I have made more money than is acceptable in Norway," he said. "I hope my announcement will make people focus on my business activities rather than on me."
Kristin Halvorsen, chairwoman of the Socialist Left Party, which is represented in parliament, was pleased with Roekke's atonement.
"It is a good thing that Roekke has realised he needs goodwill if he is to conduct serious business," she said. "But I did not know it was so easy to frighten him."
OSTENTATION CONDEMNED IN EGALITARIAN NORWAY
Eduardo Archetti, professor of social anthropology at Oslo University, said Roekke was popular with many Norwegians because he was self-made, but his mistake was his lack of humility.

"Once he started showing off his fortune like an eccentric American millionaire he lost prestige," said Archetti, who is Argentinian. "Roekke's story is the best illustration of the Jantelaw, of Norwegian values."
Norwegians pay some of the highest personal tax rates in the world, but a tax rebellion is unthinkable.

"Norwegians imagine themselves as equals. There can be no fundamental difference in the control of and access to material goods," Archetti said. "The billionaire must send his children to the same school as the electrician's kids."

Citizens may conform with egalitarian moral values and frown on success or lavish spending by individuals, but they are staunch nationalists and happily cheer on highly-paid Norwegian elite athletes at the Olympic Games and World Cup.
However, there is no contradiction.
"When Norwegians win gold medals at international sports events they do it against non-Norwegians," Archetti explained.
"It is accepted to be better than foreigners."
CHAMPIONS OF QUALITY OF LIFE

Collectively, Norwegians often see themselves as champions of the quality of life thanks to their cradle-to-grave welfare society, low crime rate, low unemployment, and beautiful landscape with steep mountains and deep fjords.

"The whole world looks up to Norway. Norway is one of the happiest countries in the world," boated a recent frontpage headline in Dagens Naeringsliv. It cited an international study on the quality of life in which Norway ranked 6th among 46 countries. "We are almost best at almost everything."
Buoyed by offshore petroleum reserves, Norway is wealthy enough to afford to stay outside the European Union. Norwegians in 1994 voted for the second time in 20 years against joining.
"There is an ideology in Norway which says no other country can match it in terms of quality of life," Archetti said.
But while Norway offers welfare, clean air and great outdoors, it levies heavy taxes on liquor, tobacco, restaurant food, petrol, cars and other items deemed as luxuries.
Half a litre of beer in an Oslo pub costs about 50 crowns.
"Norway is a place where you are punished with high prices for trying to be social and go out on the town," Archetti said. "Norwegian quality of life is about staying at home or being in nature."
($ = 7.085 Norwegian Crowns)
